unit.title: Debates and Culture
unit.summary: Where pickleball came from and why fans are passionate; scoring formats, playstyle philosophy, equipment politics, noise and court access, rating integrity, and the split pro tours.

lessons.title: Where it came from, why it exploded
lessons.objective: Tell the origin story and why the sport grew so fast.

payload.prompt: Where was pickleball first made up?

options.text: Bainbridge Island, Washington, in 1965.
A retirement community in Florida in the 1990s.
A British tennis club in the 1930s.
A Canadian hockey rink in the 1970s.

explanation.correct: A few friends on Bainbridge Island, Washington, improvised the game in 1965 with a badminton court, ping-pong-style paddles and a perforated plastic ball.
explanation.incorrect: It began in 1965 on Bainbridge Island, Washington, where a few friends invented a backyard game for their families using whatever equipment they had.
explanation.sayThisLine: It started as a backyard game on Bainbridge Island back in 1965.

payload.prompt: Complete the origin story.
payload.template: Pickleball began in the {{decade}} when a few friends on {{place}} improvised a game with spare equipment.

explanation.correct: It started in 1965 on Bainbridge Island, Washington, long before the recent boom.
explanation.incorrect: The game is older than most people think. It began in the 1960s on Bainbridge Island, Washington, as a family backyard game.
explanation.sayThisLine: It's been around since the sixties. It's just having its moment now.

payload.prompt: Everyone agrees the name came from a dog called Pickles. True?

explanation.correct: Right. One story credits the family dog, Pickles, while another says the name comes from a 'pickle boat' in rowing. People tell it both ways.
explanation.incorrect: There are two tellings: the dog named Pickles, or a 'pickle boat' of mixed-up rowers. Because people disagree, the safe line is 'it depends who you ask'.
explanation.sayThisLine: People tell the name story two ways. Which version do you like?

statement.speaker: Sam
statement.text: Pickleball is huge now and everyone has opinions about what's 'real pickleball'. Why so much drama?

payload.question: What should you say?

options.text: It's grown fast, so lots of different people want different things from it.
It's just a sport, people take it too seriously.
You should pick a side and argue your position.
The arguments don't matter, just play for fun.

payload.translation: Fast growth means beginners, rec regulars and pros all have a say, and they want different things.

followUps.line: Which debate do you hear the most at your courts?
followUps.why: Invites her to share her real opinions instead of you guessing.

followUps.line: I'm still learning, so I'd love the short version of each side.
followUps.why: Honest about your level and open to her expertise.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: You do not need to pick a side. Ask which debate she cares about and listen.

payload.prompt: Someone jokes that pickleball is only for retirees. Your move?

situation.narrative: You are at a dinner and a friend makes the joke while she is sitting right there.

facts.label: Her
facts.value: Plays a few times a week and loves it

facts.label: The joke
facts.value: Pickleball is for retirees

facts.label: What is true
facts.value: All ages play, and the pro game is young and athletic

options.label: Smile, then say it is played by every age and the pros are very athletic
options.consequence: She grins. You stayed friendly, stuck up for something she loves, and did not make it a fight.
considerations: Shows you pay attention to what she likes

options.label: Change the subject quickly
options.consequence: It avoids a scene, but she may feel you did not back her up.
considerations: Misses a chance to show support

options.label: Laugh along and add a retirement joke
options.consequence: Ouch. You just joked about the thing she loves, and in front of her.

payload.expertNote: Participation does skew older, but the game is broad and the pro scene is young. Stay cheerful and never mock players of any age.

lessons.title: Why pickleball divides
lessons.objective: Understand that the sport's growth and diversity have created real disagreements about how it should be played and governed.

statement.speaker: Sam
statement.text: Everybody at my courts argues about rules and gear. Is this normal?

payload.question: What should you say?

options.text: Probably. It's a fast-growing sport, so people care a lot about how it develops.
It's just a sport, people take it too seriously.
You should pick a side and win the argument.
The arguments don't matter, just play for fun.

payload.translation: When a sport grows quickly, different groups want different things, so rules and gear become hot topics.

followUps.line: What do people argue about the most?
followUps.why: Invites her to tell you which debates matter to her.

followUps.line: Do you have a side, or do you just enjoy watching the debate?
followUps.why: Keeps it playful and learns where she stands.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Arguments are a sign that people care. You can listen and ask questions without taking a side.

payload.prompt: Why do pickleball fans care so much about how the game is played?

options.text: Lots of people play it, so rules and culture shape their experience and the sport's future.
Professional players want control over the rules.
It's the only sport that matters.
People are naturally argumentative.

explanation.correct: The sport is big enough that rules, equipment and culture feel personal to the people who play it every week.
explanation.incorrect: It is a community, and a community cares how it develops. The debates are about the sport's future, not just one rule.
explanation.sayThisLine: With this many people playing, the debates are really about where the sport is going.

payload.prompt: Match each debate topic to what drives it.

pairs.definition: Whether side-out or rally scoring makes a better game and sport.
Whether the game should favor aggressive power or patient soft play.
Whether and how equipment should be tested to prevent unfair advantages.

distractorDefinitions: How to choose the best paddle brand
Rules that are never going to change

explanation.summary: Each debate is a real question about what makes the game fair and fun: how to score it, how to play it, and how to keep gear from deciding matches.
explanation.sayThisLine: Debates aren't noise. They're how a community decides what it values.

payload.prompt: Her open-play group is split between fun and competitive. What do you say?

situation.narrative: She is venting that her court group argues about how seriously to take it.

facts.label: Fun camp
facts.value: Casual, all levels, rotate freely

facts.label: Competitive camp
facts.value: Ratings, drills, tournaments

facts.label: Her mood
facts.value: Frustrated but still loves playing

options.label: Ask what she wants out of her pickleball
options.consequence: She thinks for a second, then opens up. You found out what matters to her without picking a side.
considerations: Different people play for different reasons
You learn what she cares about

options.label: Tell her which camp is right
options.consequence: You do not know the group, and whichever side you pick, you may be siding against her friends.
considerations: It can backfire if she disagrees

options.label: Say it's just a game and she should stop caring
options.consequence: It dismisses something she clearly cares about, so the conversation ends.

payload.expertNote: The culture debates exist because people play for different reasons. Listen first, and let her tell you which reason is hers.

payload.prompt: The USA Pickleball rulebook stays the same year to year. True?

choices.label: No, there's a new edition each year

explanation.correct: Right. USA Pickleball puts out a new rulebook edition each January, so the rules keep evolving along with the sport.
explanation.incorrect: The rulebook gets a fresh edition every January. A growing sport keeps refining its rules, and that is one reason people debate them.
explanation.sayThisLine: The rulebook gets a new edition every year, so there's always something to argue about.

lessons.title: Rally scoring vs side-out
lessons.objective: Understand why both formats have merit and why the community is divided.

payload.prompt: Side-out scoring (only server scores) is the 'real' pickleball. True?

explanation.correct: Both are valid. Side-out is the traditional way, and rally scoring is now an official option too. Each rewards different things.
explanation.incorrect: Both side-out and rally scoring are played, and rally scoring is now in the rulebook as an option. 'Real' is a matter of taste, and each has its fans.
explanation.sayThisLine: It's not which one is real. It's which one you like playing.

payload.prompt: Her league just switched to rally scoring and she is annoyed. What do you say?

situation.narrative: She tells you the league changed the format and half the players are grumbling.

facts.label: Side-out
facts.value: Only the serving side scores; long runs on serve

facts.label: Rally scoring
facts.value: Every rally scores for its winner

facts.label: Her mood
facts.value: Annoyed, wants to vent

options.label: Ask what she misses about side-out
options.consequence: She lists the big runs on serve and comebacks. You learned what she values and did not pick a side.

options.label: Agree that side-out is better
options.consequence: She feels heard, but you just picked a side in a debate you only recently learned.
considerations: Picks a side you cannot defend yet

options.label: Tell her rally scoring is obviously better
options.consequence: She feels dismissed, and you are defending a side you barely know.
considerations: Claims certainty you do not have

payload.expertNote: Rally scoring speeds up games and every rally counts. Side-out rewards strong serving runs and big comebacks. Both are legitimate, so get curious instead of choosing.

payload.prompt: Complete the scoring format comparison.
payload.template: In {{format1}}, only the {{serve}} scores. In {{format2}}, whoever wins the rally scores.

explanation.correct: Side-out: only the serving side can score. Rally scoring: the rally winner gets the point, whoever served.
explanation.incorrect: Side-out lets only the serving side score, while rally scoring gives the point to whoever wins the rally. Both are legal formats.
explanation.sayThisLine: Side-out rewards serving runs. Rally scoring counts every rally.

statement.speaker: Sam
statement.text: This tournament switched to rally scoring and half the players are upset. Is it cheating?

payload.question: What should you say?

options.text: Not cheating, just a different format. Both are played competitively.
Rally scoring IS cheating, side-out is the only real way.
It doesn't matter, both are exactly the same.
You should quit if you don't like it.

payload.translation: It is a format change, not a rule violation, and people have preferences.

followUps.line: Rally scoring counts every rally. Side-out rewards serving runs.
followUps.why: Shows you understand the real difference.

followUps.line: Do you think it changes how people play the points?
followUps.why: Invites her opinion instead of pretending to have one.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Both formats are used. If you are not sure which one an event uses, ask.

payload.prompt: Match each scoring concept to what it means.

pairs.definition: When the receiving team wins a rally and gains the serve without scoring.
Every rally is scored; whoever wins it scores, regardless of who served.
The serving team scores on their rallies; receiving team can only win the serve.

distractorDefinitions: A way to change the score if you disagree

explanation.summary: Two formats, two philosophies about what makes a good game: one rewards holding serve, the other counts every rally.
explanation.sayThisLine: Side-out makes the serve matter. Rally scoring counts every rally.

lessons.title: Bangers vs dinkers
lessons.objective: Understand the philosophical divide between aggressive and patient playstyles and why both have merit.

payload.prompt: She asks: 'Should beginners learn to bang or dink first?' Your move?

situation.narrative: She loves this debate and is testing how much you have picked up.

facts.label: Dinker view
facts.value: Soft game first; control makes power safer

facts.label: Banger view
facts.value: Pace first; be aggressive and learn fast

facts.label: Pro scene
facts.value: Top players mix both styles

options.label: Say many coaches start with the soft game, then ask what she thinks
options.consequence: She smiles and gives you her take. You shared what you have learned without claiming to be the expert.

options.label: Say you're still learning and ask how she'd teach a beginner
options.consequence: Honest and warm, though you could have offered something you have learned to keep the conversation moving.

options.label: Declare that bangers always win at the start
options.consequence: You just made a confident claim you cannot back up, and she will probably push back.

payload.expertNote: Many coaches start newer players on the soft game because control makes power safer later. It is still a debate, so share it lightly and ask for her view.

payload.prompt: Dinkers are more skilled than bangers at pickleball. True?

explanation.correct: Both take mastery. Dinking demands touch and patience, and banging demands timing and court sense.
explanation.incorrect: The best players aren't pure bangers or pure dinkers. They blend, and both skill sets are essential.
explanation.sayThisLine: Soft skills and power skills are different skills. The argument is about taste.

statement.speaker: Sam
statement.text: This guy banged everything and I got destroyed. Are bangers just not playing 'real' pickleball?

payload.question: What should you say?

options.text: Both styles are real. You faced an aggressive player, that's a challenge.
Bangers aren't real pickleball players, they're just hitting hard.
You should bang back harder.
He was cheating by playing that way.

payload.translation: Validate her experience while respecting both approaches.

followUps.line: Aggressive players force you to think differently. That's part of learning the game.
followUps.why: Shows you see this as a growth opportunity, not a complaint.

followUps.line: Do you think most top pros mix soft game and pace?
followUps.why: Checks what you have learned and invites her opinion.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Most top pros mix both styles, so be careful with any 'real pickleball' statements.

payload.prompt: Why can patient dinkers beat aggressive bangers at rec levels?

options.text: Hard swings at low balls make more unforced errors; patience keeps rallies alive.
Bangers are never allowed to win points.
Dinking is physically easier.
Bangers have worse paddles.

explanation.correct: Hitting hard at low balls is high-risk, so bangers often pop up or net the ball. Dinkers stay in the rally and let opponents make the errors.
explanation.incorrect: It comes down to risk. Power is hard to control on low balls at rec levels, while patience forces mistakes. Pros can hit hard accurately, so it plays differently there.
explanation.sayThisLine: Patience keeps you in the point. Pace is best saved for a ball you can attack.

payload.prompt: Match each playstyle to what it emphasizes.

pairs.definition: Soft kitchen play, patience, controlling the point through setup and resetting.
Aggressive pace, attacking volleys, winning through force and timing.
Mixing soft game and aggression; knowing when to be patient and when to speed up.

explanation.summary: The best players are rarely pure one style. They blend approach and timing.
explanation.sayThisLine: The soft game is the base. Speed is the finishing move.

lessons.title: Paddle technology and the spin test
lessons.objective: Understand the equipment arms race and why equipment testing is controversial.

payload.prompt: Why is paddle technology controversial in pickleball?

options.text: Paddles keep improving (more spin, more pop), and some fear gear will decide matches.
Paddles are too expensive.
Brands compete for sponsorships.
There's no controversy; everyone agrees paddles are fine.

explanation.correct: Grippier, more powerful paddles help players add spin and speed. Some welcome the innovation, and others worry about an arms race where equipment matters more than skill.
explanation.incorrect: The heart of the debate is fairness versus innovation: better paddles are exciting, but too much spin can tilt matches toward gear instead of skill.
explanation.sayThisLine: It's innovation versus fairness. Nobody wants gear to decide the match.

payload.prompt: Approved paddle faces can be as rough as the maker wants. True?

explanation.correct: Right. Approved paddles have to stay within surface limits, and testing is how governing bodies try to keep spin from running away.
explanation.incorrect: Approved paddles face limits on their surface, and the spin-rate test is part of the governing body's effort to keep gear from deciding matches.
explanation.sayThisLine: There are limits on the surface, so spin can't run away.

payload.prompt: She fears her favorite paddle might not pass the spin test. What do you say?

situation.narrative: She loves her raw carbon paddle and has just heard about the spin-rate test.

facts.label: Her paddle
facts.value: Raw carbon, and she loves it

facts.label: Her worry
facts.value: It may not stay legal

facts.label: What you know
facts.value: There is an approved list she can check

options.label: Suggest checking the approved list and ask how she feels about her options
options.consequence: She feels helped, not lectured. She can get facts, and you stayed honest about what you do not know.
considerations: Does not guess about one paddle

options.label: Tell her it'll be fine
options.consequence: Kind, but you do not actually know. If the paddle is not approved, she may feel misled.

options.label: Say the test is unfair
options.consequence: It does not help her, and you are taking a side in a debate you just learned about.

payload.expertNote: You do not need to know how the test works. Point her to the approved list, be honest about what you do not know, and let her decide.

statement.speaker: Sam
statement.text: Honestly, I think the spin test is overkill. Innovation is part of sports.

payload.question: What should you say?

options.text: That's a fair take. The other side says gear shouldn't decide matches.
You're wrong, the test is obviously right.
Nobody cares about paddles anyway.
Then you should stop playing.

payload.translation: She is on the innovation side of the paddle debate.

followUps.line: What would you want a governing body to do about spin, if anything?
followUps.why: Asks for her view instead of claiming one.

followUps.line: I've heard the fairness argument. Does it worry you at all?
followUps.why: Respectfully invites the other side without pushing it.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: You do not need to know how the test works. Name both sides and ask what she thinks.

payload.prompt: Complete the spin-test explanation.
payload.template: The spin-rate test checks how much {{what}} a paddle makes, because some fear {{worry}} could decide matches.

explanation.correct: The test looks at spin, and the worry behind it is that gear, not skill, could start deciding matches.
explanation.incorrect: It is a spin test, so it checks how much spin a paddle face produces. The concern behind it is an equipment arms race where gear beats skill.
explanation.sayThisLine: They're checking spin so gear doesn't decide matches.

lessons.title: Noise, courts and the community
lessons.objective: Understand the tension between growth and local community concerns, especially noise and court access.

payload.prompt: Your neighborhood has a noise complaint about pickleball at the public court. How do you respond?

situation.narrative: A community meeting is called. You care about the sport and the neighbors.

facts.label: Issue
facts.value: Pickleball pop is loud, especially mornings/evenings

facts.label: Context
facts.value: Court is new, community split on it

facts.label: Solutions
facts.value: Quiet hours, sound barriers, relocate, or compromise

options.label: Propose quieter hours; help with sound dampening
options.consequence: Shows respect to both communities. Limits early and late play, adds barriers, and keeps the court.

options.label: It's a public court; noise is normal
options.consequence: Dismisses neighbors and risks losing the court to complaints and ordinances.

options.label: Move the court away from residences
options.consequence: Solves noise but loses convenient access. Hard to execute unless land exists.

payload.expertNote: Noise is real, and dismissing it loses community support. Compromise keeps courts open.

payload.prompt: Noise complaints about pickleball are legitimate concerns. True?

choices.label: Yes, noise is real and affects neighbors

explanation.correct: Yes. The sharp pop carries, especially early or late in the day. Many communities now use quieter paddles and balls, sound barriers or set play hours.
explanation.incorrect: The pop is sharp and carries far, so neighbors have a point. The debate is how to balance growth with community concerns.
explanation.sayThisLine: The noise is real. Let's find a fix that keeps the courts open.

statement.speaker: Sam
statement.text: The tennis players are mad because the city converted their court to pickleball. Is that wrong?

payload.question: What should you say?

options.text: Tennis players lost their court; that's a real frustration. Both communities deserve space.
Tennis is dying, it's fine to convert all their courts.
They should just play pickleball instead.
The city should do whatever gets more players.

payload.translation: Acknowledge the tension without taking a side; respect both communities.

followUps.line: Converting courts quickly without asking people creates real resentment.
Are there other courts nearby that could be shared?
followUps.why: Moves toward a practical fix instead of a side.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Court conversions have sparked backlash in some towns. Listening to both groups beats picking a winner.

payload.prompt: Why do some cities convert tennis courts to pickleball?

options.text: Demand is high, and one tennis court can be lined for several pickleball courts.
Pickleball cannot be played on a court with a tennis net.
Tennis has been banned on public courts.
Pickleball courts must be indoors.

explanation.correct: A tennis court has room for several pickleball courts, so converting one helps many more people play. That efficiency is part of the appeal and part of the tension.
explanation.incorrect: It is about space and demand. A pickleball court is much smaller than a tennis court, so one tennis court can be lined for several. Nothing bans tennis or requires indoor courts.
explanation.sayThisLine: One tennis court can fit several pickleball courts, which is why cities do it.

payload.prompt: Your city has 20 courts and 3,000 pickleball players but noise complaints are rising. What's your priority?

situation.narrative: Growth is good but community relations matter.

facts.label: Players
facts.value: 3,000 and growing

facts.label: Courts
facts.value: 20 available, slots fill in minutes

facts.label: Complaints
facts.value: Noise, mostly early mornings and evenings

facts.label: Tennis
facts.value: 100 players on 8 courts, underused

options.label: Build new courts; quiet ones with barriers; designate quiet hours
options.consequence: Solves capacity while addressing noise. Shows the sport can be a good neighbor.

options.label: Convert all underused tennis courts to pickleball
options.consequence: Fixes court shortage but alienates tennis community and doesn't solve noise.

options.label: Limit play to midday; cap court bookings
options.consequence: Reduces conflict but frustrates 3,000 players wanting evening and early access.

payload.expertNote: The best cities plan for growth instead of reacting to complaints.

lessons.title: Ratings and integrity
lessons.objective: Understand rating systems and sandbagging concerns.

payload.prompt: A 3.0 entrant is beating every 4.0 on court. Do you say something?

situation.narrative: Rating integrity matters in tournaments, but you only see one weekend of play.

facts.label: Player
facts.value: Entered the 3.0 division and is beating everyone

facts.label: What you know
facts.value: Only what you saw this weekend

facts.label: Who can check
facts.value: The tournament director can look at results

options.label: Mention what you saw to the director, without accusing anyone
options.consequence: You shared an observation, not a verdict. The director can check results and decide.
considerations: You do not know their history
The director has the tools to check

options.label: Stay quiet; it's not your responsibility
options.consequence: Avoids conflict. The director or other players may notice anyway.

options.label: Confront them directly and call it sandbagging
options.consequence: You do not know their history, so you may accuse an improving player. It creates conflict without solving anything.

payload.expertNote: Sandbagging hurts fair competition, but players also improve fast. Share what you saw without accusing, and let the director check the record.

payload.prompt: Rating systems like DUPR have completely ended sandbagging. True?

explanation.correct: DUPR helps because it follows recorded results, but it does not eliminate sandbagging. Rating integrity is still an ongoing debate.
explanation.incorrect: A rating built from results is harder to game than a self-rating, but someone can still enter a division below their true level. The debate continues.
explanation.sayThisLine: Ratings help a lot, but people still argue about integrity.

statement.speaker: Sam
statement.text: I'm a 3.5 but my DUPR is 3.8. Should I enter a 4.0 tournament or wait?

payload.question: What should you say?

options.text: Your DUPR is a decent guide. What does your gut say?
Stay in 3.5 until DUPR hits exactly 4.0.
DUPR doesn't matter, just rate yourself whatever you want.
You'll definitely sandbag if you move up.

payload.translation: She is weighing a self-rating against a results-based rating and deciding which division fits.

followUps.line: DUPR comes from recorded match results, so it's a useful gauge of where you really are.
followUps.why: Explains the rating without making it absolute.

followUps.line: Playing up and losing is how people learn. That's different from sandbagging.
followUps.why: Frames moving up as growth, not cheating.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Moving up to play tougher opponents is growth, not sandbagging. Ask what she wants from the tournament.

payload.prompt: Match each rating concept to what it means.

pairs.definition: A player's own estimate of their skill level, often used to enter divisions.
A rating calculated from recorded match results; harder to fake than a self-rating.
Deliberately under-rating yourself to enter a lower division and gain an unfair advantage.

explanation.summary: A self-rating is your own estimate, DUPR follows recorded results, and sandbagging is deliberately entering below your level.
explanation.sayThisLine: Rate yourself honestly. Your results will show up either way.

lessons.title: Tours, contracts and the Olympics
lessons.objective: Understand the business-side debates: split tours, contracts and Olympic hopes.

payload.prompt: Why do fans argue about pro pickleball being split across tours?

options.text: With several tours, the best players are spread out and do not always meet.
Each tour plays on a different size of court.
Only one tour is allowed to use approved paddles.
The Olympics assigns players to tours.

explanation.correct: When the pro game is divided across tours, the top players, calendars and rankings can be split, so fans cannot always see the best matchups in one place.
explanation.incorrect: The worry is about the split itself: with several tours, events, rankings and stars can be divided. The court, the paddles and the rules are the same.
explanation.sayThisLine: I wish the best players all showed up in one place.

statement.speaker: Sam
statement.text: I wish all the pros would just play one tour. It's so confusing.

payload.question: What should you say?

options.text: I get that. What would you change to make it easier to follow?
It's all the same, don't overthink it.
They should be forced to join one tour.
The Olympics picks which tour each pro joins.

payload.translation: She finds the split tours confusing and wishes it were simpler to follow the stars.

followUps.line: Is it mostly the different calendars, or the different rankings?
followUps.why: Asks a specific question without pretending to know the details.

followUps.line: I'm still learning who plays where. Want to walk me through it?
followUps.why: Honest about your level and invites her to teach.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: The business side is messy and changing. Ask what she follows instead of guessing who is under contract where.

payload.prompt: One pro tour can decide pickleball joins the Olympics. True?

choices.label: Yes, a tour can decide it

explanation.correct: Right. The International Olympic Committee decides which sports are included. It looks at things like global reach and organized governance, which is why split tours come up in the debate.
explanation.incorrect: No single tour can do this. The Olympic committee chooses the sports, and it looks at how widely a sport is played and how united its governance is.
explanation.sayThisLine: The Olympic committee decides, and they care about global reach and unified governance.

payload.prompt: She says pickleball belongs in the Olympics. How do you respond?

situation.narrative: She is excited and wants to see what you think.

facts.label: Her view
facts.value: It should be an Olympic sport

facts.label: What you know
facts.value: The Olympic committee decides, weighing reach and governance

facts.label: Status
facts.value: Changes over time, so check the current news

options.label: Ask what she thinks the sport needs to get there
options.consequence: She lights up and starts listing what she thinks matters. You asked a real question and shared a little of what you know.
considerations: Uses what you learned without bluffing

options.label: Agree enthusiastically and say it is obviously happening soon
options.consequence: She enjoys the support, but you just made a prediction you cannot back up.
considerations: Claims a fact you do not know

options.label: Say it isn't a real sport
options.consequence: That is the fastest way to end the conversation. She plays it, so it is definitely real to her.

payload.expertNote: Olympic status can change, so avoid confident predictions. Ask her what she thinks matters and stay curious.

payload.prompt: Match each business-side term to what it means.

pairs.definition: The pro game being split across several tours and organizations.
A contract term limiting which tours or leagues a player may compete in.
The organization that sets and updates the rules and approves equipment.

explanation.summary: Fragmentation is the split across tours, exclusivity is what a contract can restrict, and a governing body is who writes the rules.
explanation.sayThisLine: The debate is about who plays where, and who gets to set the rules.
